sections.heading: What is amlodipine used for and how does it work?
sections.body:
Amlodipine is a calcium channel blocker. Doctors use it to treat high blood pressure. The NHS says that if you have high blood pressure, taking amlodipine can help to prevent future heart disease, heart attacks and strokes. It is also used for angina, which is chest pain caused by heart disease. MedlinePlus says it is also used for coronary artery disease, and that it helps to control these conditions but does not cure them. The NHS says it works by blocking calcium from going into the muscles of the heart and blood vessels. Muscles need calcium to contract, so blocking it makes the muscle cells relax and the blood vessels widen.

The NHS says most adults and children over the age of 6 can take amlodipine, but it is not suitable for some people. It can be taken at any time of day, but the NHS suggests keeping to about the same time each day. If side effects bother you, the NHS says a doctor may be able to prescribe a different medicine.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of amlodipine?
sections.body:
The NHS lists the common side effects of amlodipine as swelling in the ankles, feet and legs, headaches, dizziness, sleepiness, a pounding heartbeat (palpitations), flushing, feeling sick, constipation or diarrhoea, and tiredness. For swelling, the NHS suggests raising your legs when you are sitting down.

The NHS says some side effects should ease after a week or so as the body gets used to the medicine, but others can last longer. It also says that if you feel dizzy you should not drive, ride a bike or use tools or machinery until the dizziness passes. The NHS advises speaking to a doctor or pharmacist if side effects bother you or do not go away, and says a doctor may be able to prescribe a different medicine.

sections.heading: Which amlodipine side effects are serious?
sections.body:
Serious side effects are rare, according to the NHS. The NHS lists severe stomach pain, which can be a sign of an inflamed pancreas, and yellowing of the whites of the eyes or skin, which can be a sign of liver problems. The yellowing may be less obvious on brown or black skin.

The NHS says to call 999 if your lips, mouth, throat or tongue suddenly swell, or if you have difficulty breathing, because these can be signs of a serious allergic reaction. The NHS also says to call 999 for chest pain that does not go away after a few minutes, or chest pain that is new or worse in someone who already has angina. In these emergencies the NHS says not to drive yourself to A&E.

sections.heading: Grapefruit, alcohol and simvastatin with amlodipine
sections.body:
The NHS says that large amounts of grapefruit or grapefruit juice can raise the level of amlodipine in your body and make side effects worse. The NHS says alcohol can make the blood-pressure-lowering effect of amlodipine stronger. This can cause sleepiness, dizziness or a headache, so the NHS suggests limiting how much you drink. The NHS says amlodipine tablets and liquid can be taken with or without food. Apart from grapefruit and alcohol, the NHS does not list other foods or drinks to avoid.

Amlodipine can also interact with simvastatin, a statin. The UK Drug Safety Update from the MHRA says amlodipine increases exposure to simvastatin, so the maximum recommended dose of simvastatin is limited when the two medicines are taken together.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care with amlodipine?
sections.body:
The NHS says amlodipine is not suitable for everyone. It says the medicine may not suit people who have had an allergic reaction or serious side effect from amlodipine or a similar medicine before. The same NHS list names low blood pressure, heart failure, a recent heart attack and certain heart valve disease. UK patient leaflets say people with severe low blood pressure should not take it.

In pregnancy, the main NHS amlodipine page says it is not usually recommended because there are similar medicines that are safer, but it may be used if other options have failed. A more detailed NHS page says it is not thought to be harmful to the baby, although the evidence is limited. For breastfeeding, the Specialist Pharmacy Service, an NHS service, says amlodipine passes into breast milk usually in very small amounts and that no side effects have been reported in breastfed infants. One NHS page says it is acceptable if the baby is healthy, while the main page says it is not usually used when breastfeeding.

faqs.q: Does amlodipine cause ankle swelling?
faqs.a: Yes, swelling in the ankles, feet and legs is one of the common side effects listed by the NHS. For swelling, the NHS suggests raising your legs when you are sitting down. The NHS advises speaking to a doctor or pharmacist if side effects bother you or do not go away, and says a doctor may be able to prescribe a different medicine.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol while taking amlodipine?
faqs.a: The NHS says alcohol can make the blood-pressure-lowering effect of amlodipine stronger. This can cause sleepiness, dizziness or a headache. The NHS suggests limiting how much alcohol you drink. If you feel dizzy, the NHS says not to drive, ride a bike or use tools or machinery until it passes.

faqs.q: Is grapefruit a problem with amlodipine?
faqs.a: The NHS says large amounts of grapefruit or grapefruit juice can raise the amount of amlodipine in your body. That can make side effects worse. The NHS also says that if side effects bother you, a doctor may be able to prescribe a different medicine.

faqs.q: Can I take amlodipine if I am pregnant or breastfeeding?
faqs.a: The main NHS amlodipine page says it is not usually recommended in pregnancy because there are similar medicines that are safer, but it may be used if other options have failed. A more detailed NHS page says it is not thought to be harmful to the baby, although the evidence is limited. For breastfeeding, one NHS page says it is acceptable if the baby is healthy, while the main page says it is not usually used.

faqs.q: What are the serious warning signs with amlodipine?
faqs.a: The NHS says to call 999 for sudden swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, difficulty breathing, or chest pain that does not stop after a few minutes. It lists severe stomach pain and yellowing of the skin or whites of the eyes as possible signs of pancreas or liver problems. The NHS says serious side effects are rare.

sections.heading: What is amoxicillin used for?
sections.body:
Amoxicillin is a penicillin antibiotic, a medicine that treats infections caused by bacteria. The NHS says it is used for chest infections, including pneumonia, and for dental abscesses. It is often prescribed for children with ear infections. The NHS also says it can be used with other medicines for stomach ulcers.

In the UK it needs a prescription. It comes as capsules or a liquid, and the NHS says injections are usually given only in hospital. The NHS says most adults and children can take amoxicillin. For most infections, the NHS says people should feel better within a few days.

Antibiotics only work on infections caused by bacteria. They have no effect on viral illnesses such as colds and flu.

sections.heading: How does amoxicillin work?
sections.body:
Amoxicillin belongs to the penicillin group of antibiotics. Penicillin antibiotics kill susceptible bacteria by blocking an enzyme that completes the building of the bacterial cell wall.

The NHS says to tell a doctor if there is no improvement after a few days, or if symptoms get worse at any point. NHS Shropshire, Telford and Wrekin advises taking antibiotics exactly as prescribed, including the full course, and never saving them for later or sharing them with others.

Unnecessary use of antibiotics can cause some bacteria to become resistant to them, which is called antimicrobial resistance. A practice page adds that routine procedures such as surgery, cancer treatment and organ transplants become riskier as antibiotics lose their effect.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of amoxicillin?
sections.body:
The NHS lists feeling sick and diarrhoea as the most common side effects. It also says thrush can occur after antibiotics.

The NHS says to call a doctor or NHS 111 now for diarrhoea that is severe or that contains blood or mucus. It lists signs of liver problems among the serious effects, such as yellowing of the skin or eyes, and pale poo with dark urine. Some of these serious effects can appear up to two months after the course has finished.

Delayed allergic reactions can happen several days after taking amoxicillin capsules. The NHS says these are usually a mild skin rash, though a high temperature, joint pain and swollen glands can also occur.

sections.heading: Allergy and who needs extra care with amoxicillin
sections.body:
In rare cases, amoxicillin can cause a serious allergic reaction called anaphylaxis. The NHS says signs include swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat and difficulty breathing, and that anaphylaxis needs emergency treatment. In the UK, 999 is the number to call in an emergency.

The NHS lists a past allergic reaction to amoxicillin, penicillin or another medicine among the things to tell a doctor about before taking amoxicillin. The UK product information says a doctor should ask carefully about earlier allergic reactions to penicillins, cephalosporins or other related antibiotics before treatment starts.

The NHS says to check with a doctor or pharmacist before taking amoxicillin. It advises telling a doctor first about liver or kidney problems, upcoming blood or urine tests, and recent or upcoming vaccinations. Glandular fever is also on that list, because amoxicillin can cause a rash in people who have it.

The NHS says amoxicillin can be taken during pregnancy, while advising a check with a pharmacist or doctor first. It also says amoxicillin can be taken while breastfeeding, because only tiny amounts get into breast milk.

sections.heading: Taking amoxicillin with other medicines or alcohol
sections.body:
The NHS says alcohol can be drunk while taking amoxicillin. UK product information lists some medicines that can interact with amoxicillin. Allopurinol may make allergic skin reactions more likely. Probenecid reduces the kidneys' removal of amoxicillin, which can raise and prolong its levels in the blood, and the product information says using the two together is not recommended. Blood thinners such as warfarin may call for extra blood tests. Methotrexate may increase side effects, and other antibiotics such as tetracycline may make amoxicillin work less well.

The NHS says amoxicillin does not stop any type of contraception working, including the combined pill, the progestogen-only pill and emergency contraception. However, being sick or having severe or long-lasting diarrhoea may stop contraceptive pills protecting against pregnancy. The NHS says amoxicillin should not affect the ability to drive or cycle.

faqs.q: Can alcohol be drunk while taking amoxicillin?
faqs.a: The NHS says alcohol can be drunk while taking amoxicillin. It also says amoxicillin should not affect the ability to drive or cycle. The most common side effects the NHS lists are feeling sick and diarrhoea, and the NHS says thrush can occur after antibiotics. These answers come from the NHS page about amoxicillin itself.

faqs.q: Does amoxicillin work for colds and flu?
faqs.a: No, antibiotics only work on infections caused by bacteria. Colds and flu are viral illnesses, and antibiotics have no effect on them. The NHS says GPs do not recommend antibiotics for colds and flu because they will not relieve symptoms or speed up recovery. Unnecessary use of antibiotics can cause some bacteria to become resistant to them, which is called antimicrobial resistance.

faqs.q: What if amoxicillin does not seem to help?
faqs.a: The NHS says to tell a doctor if there is no improvement after a few days, or if symptoms get worse at any point. For most infections, the NHS says people should feel better within a few days. NHS Shropshire, Telford and Wrekin advises taking antibiotics exactly as prescribed, including the full course.

faqs.q: Does amoxicillin affect the contraceptive pill?
faqs.a: The NHS says amoxicillin does not stop any type of contraception working, including the combined pill, the progestogen-only pill and emergency contraception. The exception is when it makes someone sick or causes severe or long-lasting diarrhoea, because contraceptive pills may then not protect against pregnancy.

faqs.q: What can cause a rash during amoxicillin treatment?
faqs.a: The NHS says amoxicillin can cause a rash in people with glandular fever. Delayed allergic reactions can happen several days after taking amoxicillin capsules and are usually a mild skin rash, though a high temperature, joint pain and swollen glands can also occur. Swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat, or difficulty breathing, may be anaphylaxis, which needs emergency treatment: call 999.

sections.heading: What is aspirin used for?
sections.body:
Aspirin belongs to a group of medicines called non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, or NSAIDs. The NHS describes low-dose aspirin as a medicine that lowers the risk of heart attacks and strokes in people who are at high risk of them. Examples of people at high risk are those who have already had a heart attack or stroke, or who have angina. The NHS also describes low-dose aspirin being used to help prevent pre-eclampsia, a complication of pregnancy. Aspirin is also used for pain relief, and the NHS gives separate information for that use.

The NHS says most people aged 16 and over can take low-dose aspirin if a doctor recommends it. It also says that, for people who do not have heart disease and are not at high risk of it, the risk of side effects, particularly bleeding, outweighs the benefit. To prevent a heart attack or stroke, the NHS says people usually need to take it for a long time, sometimes for life.

sections.heading: How does aspirin work?
sections.body:
Platelets are tiny blood cells that clump together to help blood form a clot. Research papers describe aspirin as acting on an enzyme in platelets called COX-1. By blocking this enzyme, aspirin cuts the production of thromboxane A2, a chemical signal that drives platelets to clump together.

Platelets cannot make new COX enzyme, so aspirin's effect on them is prolonged. The research describes platelet clumping as recovering only as new platelets are made, which is why the effect lasts for days. The NHS describes low-dose aspirin as helping to prevent heart attacks and strokes in people at high risk, and treats it as a different use from aspirin for pain relief.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of aspirin?
sections.body:
The NHS says indigestion and stomach aches are the most common side effects of low-dose aspirin. Aspirin can also make people bleed more easily, so there may be nosebleeds and easier bruising, and a cut may take longer than normal to stop bleeding. Indigestion that does not go away could be a sign that aspirin has caused a stomach ulcer, and the NHS advises speaking to a GP or pharmacist about it.

The NHS says to call a doctor or NHS 111 straight away for coughing up blood, or for blood in the pee, poo or vomit. It also lists yellow skin or eyes, darker urine, painful joints, and swollen hands or feet as reasons to call. The NHS says to call 999 for sudden swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, fast or difficult breathing, or a tight throat.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care with aspirin?
sections.body:
The NHS describes a possible link between aspirin and Reye's syndrome in children, and advises against giving aspirin to children under 16 unless a doctor says to. The NHS says low-dose aspirin is given to children only when a doctor prescribes it, for example after heart surgery or for Kawasaki disease.

The NHS says some adults should talk to a doctor before taking low-dose aspirin, including people who have had a stomach ulcer, or who have asthma or lung disease, a bleeding or clotting problem, liver or kidney problems, or gout. A past allergy to aspirin or similar painkillers, and a recent stroke, are also on the list. The NHS says low-dose aspirin may not mix well with many herbal products, and names turmeric as one that may raise the risk of bleeding. It also says taking it with other blood thinners, such as clopidogrel or warfarin, can raise the risk of bleeding.

faqs.q: Can children take aspirin?
faqs.a: The NHS advises against giving aspirin to children under 16 unless a doctor says to, because of a possible link with Reye's syndrome. The NHS says Reye's syndrome most commonly affects children between 5 and 14 years of age. It gives after heart surgery and Kawasaki disease as examples of when a doctor may prescribe low-dose aspirin to a child.

faqs.q: Can aspirin be taken in pregnancy or while breastfeeding?
faqs.a: The NHS says low-dose aspirin is taken in pregnancy only if a specialist, midwife, GP or fertility doctor advises it, and that higher-dose aspirin for pain relief is not recommended. While breastfeeding, it says to take it only if a doctor has advised it. Only trace amounts reach breast milk and are unlikely to harm the baby, although there is a possible link with Reye's syndrome.

faqs.q: Do people have to take low-dose aspirin for life?
faqs.a: To prevent a heart attack or stroke, the NHS says people usually need to take low-dose aspirin for a long time, sometimes for life, and that it works best when taken for many months and years. It stresses that the medicine is taken exactly as the doctor recommends. The NHS advises speaking to a GP or pharmacist about indigestion that does not go away.

faqs.q: Which side effects need urgent help?
faqs.a: The NHS says to call 999 for sudden swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, fast or difficult breathing, or a tight throat. It says to call a doctor or NHS 111 straight away for coughing up blood, or for blood in the pee, poo or vomit.

sections.heading: What is atorvastatin used for?
sections.body:
Atorvastatin is a cholesterol-lowering medicine called a statin. MedlinePlus says it belongs to a group of medicines known as HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors. The NHS says it is used to treat high cholesterol. High cholesterol can cause problems with the heart and blood vessels, known as cardiovascular disease. Atorvastatin is also used to help prevent heart attacks and strokes.

The NHS says a doctor decides how much to prescribe, based on why it is needed, the cholesterol level and the other medicines a person takes. The NHS also says a person still gets the benefits of the medicine when they feel well. If atorvastatin is stopped, cholesterol levels may go up again. The NHS therefore says to talk to a doctor first if stopping is being considered because of a suspected side effect.

sections.heading: How does atorvastatin work and how quickly?
sections.body:
Atorvastatin works by stopping the liver from making cholesterol, which lowers the amount of cholesterol in the blood. LDL is one of the types of cholesterol carried in the blood. The NHS says cholesterol levels should fall within 4 weeks if the medicine is taken regularly as prescribed.

The NHS says routine liver blood tests are offered during the first 12 months of treatment. These are done to check that the liver is working properly. The NHS says atorvastatin can be taken with or without food. The NHS says that if it is stopped, cholesterol levels may go up again. It also says a person who suspects a side effect should talk to a doctor first, because the doctor can check whether atorvastatin is the cause or whether the problem is unrelated.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of atorvastatin?
sections.body:
The NHS lists headache, dizziness, feeling sick, muscle aches with swollen joints, and sleep problems among the common side effects. The NHS says atorvastatin can sometimes cause serious side effects, although most of them are rare. These include inflammation of the liver or pancreas, and inflammation and damage to the muscles.

Muscle problems can cause cramps, severe pain and weakness, and sometimes a high temperature and red or brown pee. Inflammation of the liver can cause yellowing of the skin and the whites of the eyes, which may be harder to see on brown or black skin. Inflammation of the pancreas can cause severe stomach pain.

A serious allergic reaction is an emergency. The NHS says to call 999 if the lips, mouth, throat or tongue suddenly swell, or if breathing or swallowing becomes difficult, and not to drive to A&E. For other suspected side effects, the NHS says to talk to a doctor first, who can check whether atorvastatin is the cause.

sections.heading: Taking atorvastatin with other medicines, grapefruit or alcohol
sections.body:
NHS 111 Wales says statins can react with some other substances, which can raise the risk of serious side effects such as muscle damage. A patient leaflet for atorvastatin lists the antibiotic fusidic acid as a medicine that can cause serious muscle breakdown when taken with atorvastatin.

The NHS says too much grapefruit juice can raise the level of atorvastatin in the blood and increase the risk of side effects. The British Heart Foundation says people taking atorvastatin can have grapefruit occasionally, but not in large amounts. It says the advice differs between statins, and that people taking simvastatin are advised to avoid grapefruit altogether.

The NHS also lists regularly drinking a lot of alcohol among the reasons a person may not be suitable for atorvastatin.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care with atorvastatin?
sections.body:
The NHS says most adults can take atorvastatin. It may not suit people who have had an allergic reaction to atorvastatin or another statin, or who have liver or kidney problems. An underactive thyroid, past muscle side effects from a statin and muscle conditions such as myasthenia gravis are also on the list.

The NHS advises against atorvastatin in pregnancy and advises stopping it some months before trying to conceive. On breastfeeding, the NHS says a person may be able to take it but should check with a pharmacist or doctor first. NHS 111 Wales is stricter and says statins should not be taken by anyone who is pregnant or breastfeeding. The British Heart Foundation also says statins should not be taken during pregnancy.

faqs.q: Can grapefruit juice be drunk with atorvastatin?
faqs.a: The NHS says too much grapefruit juice can raise the level of atorvastatin in the blood and increase the risk of side effects. The British Heart Foundation says people taking atorvastatin can have grapefruit occasionally, but not in large amounts. It says the advice differs between statins, and that people taking simvastatin are advised to avoid grapefruit altogether.

faqs.q: What happens if atorvastatin is stopped?
faqs.a: The NHS says that if atorvastatin is stopped, cholesterol levels may go up again. It also says a person still gets the benefits when they feel well. If a side effect is suspected, the NHS says to talk to a doctor first, who can check whether atorvastatin is the cause or whether the problem is unrelated.

faqs.q: Does atorvastatin cause muscle pain?
faqs.a: The NHS lists muscle aches with swollen joints among the common side effects of atorvastatin. It lists inflammation and damage to the muscles among the serious side effects, most of which are rare. Cramps, severe pain and weakness, sometimes with a high temperature and red or brown pee, are listed as signs of this. The NHS says to talk to a doctor first if a side effect is suspected.

faqs.q: Can atorvastatin be taken in pregnancy?
faqs.a: The NHS advises against atorvastatin in pregnancy and advises stopping it some months before trying to conceive. On breastfeeding, the NHS says a person may be able to take it but should check with a pharmacist or doctor first. NHS 111 Wales is stricter and says statins should not be taken by anyone who is pregnant or breastfeeding.

faqs.q: Does atorvastatin affect the liver?
faqs.a: The NHS says routine blood tests to check the liver are offered during the first 12 months of treatment. It lists inflammation of the liver as a serious side effect, which can cause yellowing of the skin and the whites of the eyes. The NHS also lists liver problems, and regularly drinking a lot of alcohol, among the reasons atorvastatin may not suit a person.

sections.heading: What is ibuprofen used for?
sections.body: Ibuprofen is a painkiller that also treats inflammation. Inflammation is the swelling and soreness that can come with an injury or a joint problem. It belongs to a group of medicines called non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, or NSAIDs. Ibuprofen comes as tablets, capsules, granules and liquid that are swallowed, and as gel, mousse or spray that is applied to the skin. The NHS describes it as an everyday painkiller for back pain, period pain, toothache and cold or flu symptoms, and says it also treats inflammation such as sprains, strains and arthritis pain. The NHS says it does not usually work well for nerve pain, and that a doctor may need to prescribe a different medicine when pain is related to the nerves. The NHS compares ibuprofen with other painkillers, including paracetamol, aspirin and co-codamol, which combines paracetamol with low-dose codeine. It says ibuprofen can cause more side effects than paracetamol, and it has a separate page on who can and cannot take ibuprofen.

sections.heading: How does ibuprofen work?
sections.body: The NHS says ibuprofen works by lowering the amount of certain hormones in the body that cause pain and swelling. With less of these chemicals, there is less pain and less swelling. A hospital leaflet explains that tissue injury prompts the body to make chemicals called prostaglandins, which are involved in pain and inflammation, and that NSAIDs reduce their amount. A medical reference says ibuprofen blocks enzymes called cyclo-oxygenase, which reduces the making of prostaglandins and similar chemicals. The same reference says these chemicals also help to protect the stomach lining and to maintain blood flow to the kidneys, so stomach and kidney side effects trace back to the same pathway. The NHS says swallowed forms start to work soon after they are taken, while skin products take a day or two to start working. It says some people take ibuprofen for many years when a doctor prescribes it. Ulcers are a risk with long-term use or large amounts, and a doctor may prescribe a stomach-protecting medicine for people at risk. The NHS also says that someone already taking ibuprofen by mouth regularly gets no extra benefit from also using the gel.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of ibuprofen?
sections.body: The NHS lists indigestion and stomach aches, feeling sick, headaches, a rash, dizziness, and diarrhoea or constipation among the common side effects. If dizziness happens, the NHS advises against driving or riding a bike until it passes. The NHS says the gel may make the eyes, mouth, lips, nose or genital area sore if it gets there. Rarer serious effects include bleeding in the stomach and a serious allergic reaction called anaphylaxis. MedlinePlus, a US source, says ibuprofen can cause ulcers, bleeding or holes in the oesophagus, stomach or intestine, and that these can happen without warning symptoms. The NHS lists black poo, which can be a sign of bleeding in the stomach, as a serious side effect. It says swollen ankles or blood in the urine are reasons to contact a doctor or NHS 111. The NHS says swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, or fast or difficult breathing, is a reason to call 999. MedlinePlus says NSAIDs such as ibuprofen may raise the risk of a heart attack or stroke, and that the risk is higher with long-term or high-amount use.

sections.heading: Taking ibuprofen with food, alcohol or other medicines
sections.body: The NHS says tablets, capsules, granules and liquid can be taken with food or milk, which makes an upset stomach less likely. On alcohol, the NHS says it is usually not a problem to drink some, but drinking too much can irritate the stomach when ibuprofen is swallowed. MedlinePlus says heavy alcohol use is one of the things that raises the risk of ulcers and bleeding with ibuprofen. Some UK patient leaflets go further and advise avoiding alcohol, because it may add to side effects in the stomach, intestines or nervous system. The NHS says ibuprofen should not be combined with other NSAIDs such as naproxen or aspirin, because that raises the risk of serious effects such as stomach ulcers. Medical references describe several medicines that interact with ibuprofen. Ibuprofen can reduce the blood-pressure-lowering effect of ACE inhibitors and may weaken the effect of diuretics. Taking it with warfarin raises the risk of serious bleeding in the stomach and gut, and it can raise the level of lithium in the blood.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care with ibuprofen?
sections.body: The NHS lists reasons not to take ibuprofen, including a past allergic reaction to aspirin or another NSAID, pregnancy, a history of stomach ulcers, and severe heart, kidney or liver failure. MedlinePlus says the risk of ulcers and bleeding is higher with long-term use, older age, poor health, smoking or heavy alcohol use. Asthma, hay fever and allergies are listed by the NHS as conditions to check with a doctor or pharmacist about first. MedlinePlus says people who have recently had a heart attack should not take ibuprofen unless a doctor directs it. Some UK leaflets list an increased tendency to bleed as a reason not to take it. UK leaflets say it should not be taken in the last three months of pregnancy, because it could harm the unborn baby or cause problems at delivery, and may cause labour to be later or longer than expected.

faqs.q: Can ibuprofen be taken on an empty stomach?
faqs.a: The NHS says tablets, capsules, granules and liquid can be taken with food or milk, which makes an upset stomach less likely. Ulcers are a risk with long-term use or large amounts, and a doctor may prescribe a stomach-protecting medicine for people at risk. The NHS lists black poo as a serious side effect, and swollen ankles or blood in the urine as reasons to contact a doctor or NHS 111.

faqs.q: How long does ibuprofen take to work?
faqs.a: The NHS says swallowed forms start to work soon after they are taken, while gel and other skin products take a day or two. It does not usually work well for nerve pain. If pharmacy painkillers do not work, the NHS says a doctor may prescribe a stronger painkiller or suggest another treatment, such as exercise or physiotherapy.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol while taking ibuprofen?
faqs.a: The NHS says it is usually not a problem to drink some alcohol with ibuprofen, but drinking too much can irritate the stomach when it is swallowed. MedlinePlus says heavy alcohol use raises the risk of ulcers and bleeding. Some UK patient leaflets advise avoiding alcohol, because it may add to side effects in the stomach, intestines or nervous system.

faqs.q: Can ibuprofen be taken in pregnancy?
faqs.a: The NHS lists pregnancy as a reason not to take ibuprofen. UK leaflets say it should not be taken in the last three months of pregnancy, because it could harm the unborn baby or cause problems at delivery. They also say it should generally not be used in the first six months unless a doctor judges it necessary.

sections.heading: What is metformin used for and how does it work?
sections.body:
Metformin is a medicine that is used to treat type 2 diabetes. The NHS says it can also be used for gestational diabetes and for polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS), the name the NHS now uses for what was previously called polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). It is also used to help prevent type 2 diabetes in people at high risk of developing it. Gestational diabetes is diabetes that first appears during pregnancy.

The NHS says metformin lowers blood sugar levels by improving the way the body handles insulin. Other descriptions add that it reduces how much glucose the liver releases. For PMOS, the NHS says it works by lowering insulin and blood sugar levels, and that it can improve ovulation and encourage regular periods, even in people without diabetes. The NHS says this use is not officially approved. It comes as standard tablets, which release metformin quickly, and as slow-release tablets, which work gradually.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of metformin?
sections.body:
The NHS lists feeling or being sick, diarrhoea, tummy pain and loss of appetite among the common side effects. A change in taste is also listed. The NHS says most of these ease after a couple of weeks. The NHS advises taking metformin with a meal to reduce side effects. Vitamin B12 deficiency is also listed as a side effect and is more likely with long-term use. Doctors may check vitamin B12 levels with a blood test in some people who take metformin for a long time.

Lactic acidosis, a build-up of acid in the blood, is a very rare but serious side effect. Symptoms the NHS lists include being sick, stomach pain, muscle cramps, breathing problems and severe tiredness. The NHS says to call 999 if lactic acidosis or a severe allergic reaction is suspected. For other serious side effects, such as inflammation of the liver, the NHS says to call NHS 111. A UK patient leaflet says lactic acidosis can lead to serious illness that needs hospital care.

sections.heading: Taking metformin with alcohol, other illnesses or before scans
sections.body:
The NHS advises limiting how much alcohol is drunk while taking metformin, because it can increase the risk of serious side effects. UK leaflets say drinking too much alcohol may increase the risk of lactic acidosis.

A UK patient leaflet says metformin is stopped before or at the time of an injection of contrast dye, and the doctor says when to restart. A review of manufacturers' labels found that all of them advise stopping metformin before scans that use contrast dye. UK patient leaflets say metformin is stopped for a short time with a condition that may cause dehydration, such as severe vomiting or diarrhoea. The NHS says that anyone who has taken more than the prescribed amount should call NHS 111. The NHS also says that if metformin causes vomiting or severe diarrhoea for more than 24 hours, contraceptive pills may not protect against pregnancy.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care with metformin?
sections.body:
The NHS says most adults and children aged 10 years and over can take metformin, but some people should tell the doctor first. These include people with uncontrolled diabetes, liver or kidney problems, a severe infection, heart failure or a high alcohol intake. A past allergic reaction to metformin is also on the NHS list.

The risk of lactic acidosis is higher when the kidneys do not work well, UK patient leaflets say. The same leaflets say the doctor checks how well the kidneys work regularly during treatment. The NHS says that if blood sugar levels are stable, metformin should not affect the ability to drive, cycle or use machinery and tools. The NHS says the risk comes from other diabetes medicines that can lower blood sugar. Metformin on its own does not cause blood sugar to fall below normal, according to an NHS Scotland resource.

sections.heading: Metformin in pregnancy and breastfeeding
sections.body:
The NHS says metformin can be taken in pregnancy, but advises checking with a doctor first. The NHS says that in gestational diabetes, medicines taken to control blood sugar are usually stopped after the baby is born.

The NHS says that if the doctor or midwife says the baby is healthy, metformin can be taken while breastfeeding. Only tiny amounts pass into breast milk, the NHS says. A review of manufacturers' labels found that they advise against metformin during breastfeeding, which differs from the NHS advice. The NHS says a health professional should be contacted if a breastfed baby feeds poorly or seems unusually drowsy or restless.

faqs.q: Can metformin cause lactic acidosis?
faqs.a: Lactic acidosis is a very rare but serious side effect. The NHS lists being sick, stomach pain, muscle cramps, breathing problems and severe tiredness as symptoms. It says to call 999 if lactic acidosis is suspected. UK patient leaflets say the risk is higher when the kidneys do not work well, and that heavy drinking may also raise it.

faqs.q: How can the stomach side effects of metformin be eased?
faqs.a: The NHS says the most common side effects are feeling or being sick, diarrhoea, tummy pain and loss of appetite. It advises taking metformin with a meal to reduce them, and says most side effects ease after a couple of weeks. Standard tablets release metformin quickly, while slow-release tablets work gradually.

faqs.q: Can alcohol be drunk while taking metformin?
faqs.a: The NHS advises limiting how much alcohol is drunk while taking metformin, because it can increase the risk of serious side effects. UK leaflets link drinking too much alcohol to a higher risk of lactic acidosis. The NHS asks people who drink heavily to tell the doctor before starting the medicine.

faqs.q: Can metformin cause vitamin B12 deficiency?
faqs.a: The NHS lists vitamin B12 deficiency among the side effects of metformin, and it is more likely with long-term use. Because of this, doctors may check vitamin B12 levels with a blood test in some people who take metformin for a long time. The common stomach side effects are separate, and most of them ease after a couple of weeks, the NHS says.

sections.heading: What is omeprazole used for?
sections.body:
Omeprazole is a proton pump inhibitor, a medicine that lowers the amount of acid the stomach makes. The NHS says it is used to treat or prevent stomach ulcers, heartburn and gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, often called GORD. It is also used, together with antibiotics, to treat a stomach infection called Helicobacter pylori.

Omeprazole comes as capsules, tablets and a liquid, and the NHS says tablets and capsules are swallowed whole with water or squash. The NHS says capsules are prescription only, while some tablets can be bought from pharmacies and supermarkets for adults. Tablets bought this way are meant for short-term use, and the NHS says to tell a doctor if symptoms persist. The NHS describes omeprazole as a medicine to treat heartburn and indigestion.

sections.heading: How does omeprazole work, and how quickly?
sections.body:
Omeprazole blocks the last step in the making of stomach acid. It acts on an enzyme called the proton pump, which sits on acid-making cells in the stomach wall. A review of its pharmacology says omeprazole is a prodrug, changed to its active form only in the acid-making cells, where it binds irreversibly to the proton pump. This gives an effective and long-lasting reduction in stomach acid.

The NHS says omeprazole starts to work within 2 to 3 days, but it may take up to 4 weeks to work fully. It is a medicine that lowers stomach acid, and the NHS lists ulcers, heartburn and GORD among the conditions it treats or prevents.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of omeprazole?
sections.body:
The NHS lists headache, stomach pain, feeling or being sick, constipation and diarrhoea as common side effects. The NHS says omeprazole can also cause dizziness, sleepiness or blurred vision, and advises against driving, cycling or using machinery or tools until feeling better.

Serious side effects are rarer. The NHS says omeprazole may affect how the body absorbs vitamin B12, particularly with long use, that taking it for more than a year may raise the chance of bone fractures, and that a serious allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) is possible in rare cases. The NHS says the level of magnesium in the blood may also fall with longer use. Anaphylaxis is a medical emergency, and the route for that in the UK is 999.

The NHS says to speak to a doctor about trouble swallowing, feeling or being sick, feeling full very quickly when eating, or losing weight without trying, because these can be signs of stomach cancer.

sections.heading: Taking omeprazole with other medicines or alcohol
sections.body:
The NHS says omeprazole can interact with other medicines, so a pharmacist or doctor can be asked about anything new. UK drug safety guidance discourages using omeprazole or esomeprazole with clopidogrel, an antiplatelet medicine. The Specialist Pharmacy Service, part of the NHS, explains that clopidogrel is activated by an enzyme called CYP2C19, and that omeprazole and esomeprazole inhibit this enzyme, which can lower the level of activated clopidogrel. The Specialist Pharmacy Service says lansoprazole, pantoprazole or rabeprazole are preferred to omeprazole for people taking clopidogrel.

The NHS says alcohol does not stop omeprazole working. But alcohol makes the stomach produce more acid than usual, which can irritate the stomach lining and make symptoms worse. For that reason the NHS says it is best to avoid alcohol if possible while taking omeprazole.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care with omeprazole?
sections.body:
The NHS lists kidney conditions, liver conditions, osteoporosis, and a past allergic reaction or serious side effect from omeprazole or another proton pump inhibitor as reasons to check with a doctor or pharmacist before taking it. The NHS says that after more than a year of omeprazole, a doctor will regularly check health to see whether to carry on.

The NHS says omeprazole can usually be taken in pregnancy, but a pharmacist or doctor should be asked first. It suggests trying to ease indigestion without medicine first. On breastfeeding, the NHS says omeprazole passes into breast milk in small amounts, and that it is OK to take while breastfeeding if a doctor or health visitor says the baby is healthy. The NHS says there is no clear evidence that omeprazole lowers fertility in men or women.

faqs.q: Can I buy omeprazole without a prescription?
faqs.a: The NHS says some omeprazole tablets can be bought from pharmacies and supermarkets for adults, while capsules are prescription only. Tablets bought this way are meant for short-term use. The NHS says to tell a doctor if symptoms persist, and that a doctor may order tests or suggest a different medicine.

faqs.q: How long does omeprazole take to work?
faqs.a: The NHS says omeprazole starts to work within 2 to 3 days, but it may take up to 4 weeks to work fully. Tablets bought from a pharmacy are meant for short-term use, and the NHS says to tell a doctor if symptoms persist. The NHS also says it is not known whether omeprazole works less well the longer it is taken.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol while taking omeprazole?
faqs.a: The NHS says alcohol does not interfere with how omeprazole works. However, alcohol makes the stomach produce more acid than usual. That extra acid can irritate the stomach lining and make symptoms worse. The NHS therefore says it is best to avoid alcohol if possible while taking omeprazole.

faqs.q: What does the NHS say about long-term use of omeprazole?
faqs.a: The NHS says taking omeprazole for more than a year may raise the chance of bone fractures and gut infections. It may also affect how the body absorbs vitamin B12. The NHS says a doctor will regularly check health after a year to see whether to carry on. The NHS also says magnesium levels in the blood may fall with longer use.

faqs.q: Which symptoms does the NHS say to mention to a doctor while taking omeprazole?
faqs.a: The NHS says to speak to a doctor about trouble swallowing, feeling or being sick, feeling full very quickly when eating, or losing weight without trying, because these can be signs of stomach cancer. The NHS also says a doctor will regularly check health after a year of omeprazole, to see whether to carry on.

sections.heading: What is paracetamol and how does it work?
sections.body:
The NHS describes paracetamol as a painkiller that is also used for a high temperature. It is used to ease pain. Paracetamol is sold in pharmacies and shops, and some types are only available on prescription. The NHS lists tablets and capsules, a liquid, tablets that are swallowed whole and dissolvable tablets.

The NHS says paracetamol seems to work by blocking chemical messengers in the brain that tell the body it is in pain. It also lowers a high temperature. A dose can take up to an hour to start working, and the effect lasts for some hours. The NHS says paracetamol can be taken with or without food, and that people can eat and drink normally while taking it. Too much paracetamol can damage the liver, according to the NHS.

Paracetamol is also one ingredient in some combined painkillers, such as co-codamol, which pairs it with codeine. The NHS says other medicines containing paracetamol, such as some cold and flu remedies, should not be taken alongside it because of the risk of overdose.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of paracetamol?
sections.body:
The NHS says serious side effects of paracetamol are rare. The main serious ones are an allergic reaction, liver problems and a problem with blood cells. A swollen throat or tongue, a raised and itchy rash, or difficulty breathing can be signs of a serious allergic reaction (anaphylaxis), and NHS 111 Wales says to call 999 or go to A&E. Feeling sick and yellowing of the skin or the whites of the eyes can be signs of liver problems, and yellowing may be harder to notice on black or brown skin. Easy bruising or nosebleeds can be signs of a problem with blood cells. A leaflet for a UK paracetamol brand advises contacting a doctor about unexpected bruising or bleeding.

Taking an extra dose is unlikely to cause problems, the NHS says, but it advises getting medical advice because too much can sometimes damage the liver.

sections.heading: Taking paracetamol with other medicines or alcohol
sections.body:
The NHS says paracetamol should not be taken with other medicines that contain paracetamol, because of the risk of overdose. UK product information says that metoclopramide and domperidone make paracetamol be absorbed faster. It also lists alcohol and some other medicines, such as barbiturates and tricyclic antidepressants, as things that may raise the risk of liver harm, especially after an overdose.

Product information also says that prolonged regular use of paracetamol may enhance the effect of warfarin and related anticoagulants, raising the risk of bleeding, while occasional doses have no significant effect. NHS 111 Wales advises people who take warfarin to check with a doctor or pharmacist, because regular paracetamol can raise the risk of bleeding.

On alcohol, the NHS says drinking a small amount is usually acceptable with paracetamol. It adds that drinking may not be suitable for people with some conditions, such as liver problems.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care, and for how long can it be used?
sections.body:
The NHS says most adults can take paracetamol, but it is not suitable for everyone. It lists people who have had an allergic reaction to it, people with kidney or liver conditions, and people who drink alcohol heavily or binge drink. NHS 111 Wales advises people with a low body weight to check with a doctor or pharmacist, and the NHS says a lower dose may be needed.

NHS 111 Wales says paracetamol can be taken during pregnancy and while breastfeeding at the recommended amount. It also says there is no good evidence that paracetamol reduces fertility in men or women.

The NHS says paracetamol can be taken regularly for many years if the recommended amount is not exceeded. For short-term self-treatment, the NHS says it should not be used for more than a few days unless a doctor advises it.

faqs.q: Can paracetamol be taken with or without food?
faqs.a: The NHS says paracetamol can be taken with or without food, and that people can eat and drink normally while taking it. A dose can take up to an hour to start working. The NHS lists tablets that are swallowed whole, dissolvable tablets, capsules and a liquid.

faqs.q: What happens if too much paracetamol is taken?
faqs.a: The NHS says an extra dose is unlikely to cause problems, but too much can sometimes damage the liver, so it advises getting medical advice. It advises calling NHS 111 if more has been taken than the packet or leaflet says, even if the person feels well. NHS hospital leaflets say many people feel well in the early stages of an overdose. If told to go to A&E, the NHS says not to drive there: ask someone else to drive, or call 999 for an ambulance.

faqs.q: Can paracetamol be taken for a long time?
faqs.a: The NHS says paracetamol can be taken regularly for many years if the recommended amount is not exceeded. For short-term self-treatment, the NHS says it should not be used for more than a few days unless a doctor advises it. Some types are only available on prescription. The NHS also says it is not suitable for people who drink alcohol heavily, and that people with a low body weight may need a lower dose.

faqs.q: Is paracetamol suitable in pregnancy or when trying for a baby?
faqs.a: NHS 111 Wales says there is no good evidence that paracetamol reduces fertility in men or women. It also says paracetamol can be taken during pregnancy and breastfeeding at recommended amounts. The NHS says most adults can take paracetamol, but it is not suitable for everyone, including people who have had an allergic reaction to it or who have kidney or liver conditions.

sections.heading: What is ramipril used for?
sections.body: The NHS describes ramipril as a medicine widely used to treat high blood pressure and heart failure. It is also prescribed after a heart attack, and the NHS says it helps prevent future strokes, heart attacks and kidney problems. The NHS says a person taking ramipril for high blood pressure may not feel any different, but this does not mean the medicine is not working. According to the NHS, ramipril starts to lower high blood pressure within a few hours, but it may take a few weeks to work fully. The NHS says ramipril is generally used long term, and that blood pressure could rise again if it is stopped. Ramipril comes in several forms, including capsules, tablets and an oral solution, which is a liquid. UK patient leaflets say the safety and effectiveness of ramipril capsules in children has not been established. The NHS has separate pages on ramipril side effects, on pregnancy, breastfeeding and fertility, and on taking it with other medicines, which can be read alongside this article. MedlinePlus, a US health site, also has a drug information page on ramipril.

sections.heading: How does ramipril work?
sections.body: Ramipril belongs to a group of medicines called ACE inhibitors, the NHS says. The NHS says ramipril relaxes and widens the blood vessels, which lowers blood pressure and makes it easier for the heart to pump blood around the body. StatPearls, a medical reference on the NCBI Bookshelf, says ramipril and its active form, ramiprilat, block an enzyme called ACE. ACE also breaks down a substance called bradykinin, so blocking it raises bradykinin levels, which StatPearls links to the dry cough. StatPearls says the cough usually starts somewhere between a week and six months after an ACE inhibitor is started. UK labelling says high potassium in the blood can occur in people with impaired kidney function or those taking potassium supplements, including salt substitutes, potassium-sparing diuretics, trimethoprim or co-trimoxazole. The same labelling notes that blood potassium usually stays within normal limits, although high potassium may occur in some people.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of ramipril?
sections.body: The NHS describes a dry cough as the most common side effect of ramipril. The NHS says cough medicines do not usually help a cough caused by ramipril. Sometimes the cough gets better on its own if the person keeps taking ramipril, the NHS says. If the cough is bothersome, the NHS says a doctor might suggest changing to a different medicine. StatPearls says angiotensin receptor blockers cause much less cough than ACE inhibitors, which is why they are often used as an alternative. The NHS lists feeling dizzy and headaches among the common side effects, and says the very first dose may make a person feel dizzy. The NHS says to call 999 now if the lips, mouth, throat or tongue suddenly swell, or if someone is breathing very fast, struggling to breathe, or has a tight throat or difficulty swallowing. The NHS says swelling of the lips, tongue and face may signal angioedema, and that people with Black skin have a higher chance of getting it. A UK patient leaflet says swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat can happen at any time during treatment.

sections.heading: Taking ramipril with other medicines, alcohol or salt substitutes
sections.body: A UK patient leaflet says that medicines used to lower blood pressure and alcohol can have additive effects. The NHS says alcohol can make dizziness worse, and advises not drinking alcohol until a person sees how ramipril affects them. UK leaflets say anti-inflammatory painkillers (NSAIDs) such as ibuprofen can make ramipril work less well. The NHS says daily low-dose aspirin can be taken with ramipril. UK leaflets list spironolactone among the medicines that can increase the amount of potassium in the blood. MedlinePlus advises talking to a doctor before using salt substitutes that contain potassium. UK labelling says ramipril can raise lithium levels in the blood, and that it may lower blood sugar, so people using insulin or diabetes tablets need close monitoring. UK leaflets list sacubitril/valsartan as a medicine to avoid combining with ramipril.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, breastfeeding and who needs extra care
sections.body: The NHS does not recommend ramipril in pregnancy, and says anyone trying to conceive should talk to a doctor first. The NHS also advises planning any pregnancy with a GP or specialist. The NHS says there is no clear evidence that ramipril reduces fertility in either men or women. According to the NHS, ramipril does not affect any type of contraception, but vomiting or prolonged diarrhoea can make contraceptive pills less reliable. The NHS says some hormonal contraception, such as the combined pill and the contraceptive patch, is not usually recommended for people with high blood pressure. On breastfeeding, the NHS says ramipril can be taken, but a person should talk to a doctor or pharmacist first, and it says the medicine is best avoided if the baby was born prematurely. The NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service says ramipril can be used with caution during breastfeeding, but enalapril is preferred, and that this applies to healthy full-term babies only. UK labelling says ramipril should not be used by people with a history of angioedema linked to ACE inhibitors, or with abnormally low or unstable blood pressure. A UK patient leaflet says dialysis or other types of blood filtering may make ramipril unsuitable, depending on the machine used.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol while taking ramipril?
faqs.a: A UK patient leaflet says that blood-pressure medicines and alcohol can have additive effects. The NHS says alcohol can make dizziness worse. The NHS advises not drinking alcohol until a person sees how ramipril affects them. It also says the very first dose may make a person feel dizzy.

faqs.q: Is swelling of the face an emergency?
faqs.a: Sudden swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue can be a sign of angioedema. The NHS says to call 999 now if this happens. The NHS gives the same advice if someone is breathing very fast, struggling to breathe, or has a tight throat or difficulty swallowing. Swelling in the throat can make breathing difficult. A UK patient leaflet says swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat can happen at any time during treatment.

faqs.q: What if ramipril gives me a cough?
faqs.a: A dry cough is the most common side effect of ramipril, the NHS says. Sometimes it gets better on its own if the person keeps taking ramipril. The NHS says cough medicines do not usually help, and that if the cough is bothersome a doctor might suggest a different medicine. StatPearls says that after an ACE inhibitor is stopped, the cough usually goes within one to four days, although it can last up to a month.

faqs.q: Can I take ibuprofen or use a salt substitute?
faqs.a: UK leaflets say anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen can make ramipril work less well. The NHS says daily low-dose aspirin can be taken with ramipril. MedlinePlus advises talking to a doctor before using salt substitutes that contain potassium. UK leaflets also list spironolactone among the medicines that can increase the amount of potassium in the blood.

faqs.q: Can ramipril be taken in pregnancy?
faqs.a: The NHS does not recommend ramipril in pregnancy. The NHS says anyone trying to conceive should talk to a doctor first, and advises planning any pregnancy with a GP or specialist. It also says there is no clear evidence that ramipril reduces fertility in either men or women.

sections.heading: What is sertraline used for and how does it work?
sections.body:
Sertraline is an antidepressant from a group called selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, or SSRIs. The NHS says it is often used for depression and sometimes for panic attacks, obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD) and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). MedlinePlus also lists social anxiety disorder among its uses. The NHS says children aged 6 to 17 can also take sertraline, but only for OCD. It comes as tablets.

The NHS says it is not known exactly how antidepressants work. One view is that they increase the levels of brain chemicals called neurotransmitters, mainly serotonin and noradrenaline. The NHS says people may start to feel better after 1 to 2 weeks, but sertraline usually takes 4 to 6 weeks to work fully.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of sertraline?
sections.body:
The NHS lists headaches, feeling sick, dizziness or drowsiness, dry mouth, diarrhoea, problems sleeping and sexual problems among the common side effects of sertraline. The NHS says some of the common side effects gradually improve as the body gets used to the medicine. It also lists agitation, shakiness and anxiety among the early side effects of antidepressants, which generally improve with time.

Serious reactions are rarer. The NHS lists serotonin syndrome and mania among them, and describes serotonin syndrome as an uncommon but potentially serious set of side effects linked to SSRIs.

MedlinePlus warns that sertraline may raise the risk of suicidal thoughts and actions in children, teenagers and young adults, and that the risk may be higher in the first few months of treatment and when the dose is increased. It lists new or worsening depression, thoughts of harming yourself, extreme worry, panic attacks and severe restlessness as warning signs, and advises calling a doctor right away if they appear. The NHS says that anyone who may be about to harm themselves should call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent mental health help, NHS 111 has a mental health option (option 2), and Samaritans is free to call on 116 123 at any time. A GP can also be asked for an emergency appointment.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care with sertraline, and what should it not be mixed with?
sections.body:
The NHS says most adults can take sertraline. People who have had an allergic reaction to sertraline or another medicine may not be able to take it. The NHS also lists heart problems, glaucoma and epilepsy as reasons for extra care, because sertraline can affect heart rhythm, raise the pressure in the eye or increase the risk of a seizure. Sertraline can make blood sugar harder to control, so a doctor may suggest checking it more often at first for people with diabetes.

The NHS says it is best not to drink alcohol while taking sertraline, because alcohol can stop the medicine working properly. Grapefruit juice can increase the amount of sertraline in the body and the risk of side effects. The NHS says not to take the herbal remedy St John's wort during treatment, because this increases the risk of side effects, and that there is very little information about other herbal remedies and supplements. The NHS flags medicines that affect the heartbeat, and other antidepressants, as ones to raise with a doctor first. The UK patient leaflet says sertraline must not be used with a group of antidepressants called MAOIs, such as selegiline or moclobemide, or with linezolid.

sections.heading: Can sertraline be taken in pregnancy or while breastfeeding?
sections.body:
The NHS says sertraline can be taken in pregnancy. Some studies have suggested that it might occasionally affect the development of a baby's heart. The NHS says that if there is any risk it is small, and that most babies born to women taking sertraline have a normal heart.

When it is taken in the weeks before delivery, sertraline can sometimes cause short-term withdrawal symptoms in the baby and, very rarely, breathing problems. The NHS says the baby will be checked after birth and given extra care if needed. MedlinePlus advises telling a doctor about a pregnancy, a plan to become pregnant or breastfeeding.

The NHS says that if a doctor or health visitor says the baby is healthy, it is OK to take sertraline while breastfeeding, and describes it as one of the preferred antidepressants during breastfeeding.

sections.heading: How is stopping sertraline managed?
sections.body:
The NHS says stopping sertraline should involve reducing the dose gradually, which helps to prevent withdrawal symptoms. The NHS says this is normally done over several weeks or months, and the pace depends on the medicine, the dose and how long it has been taken. The UK patient leaflet says not to stop taking sertraline unless a doctor says so.

The NHS says withdrawal symptoms usually begin within 5 days of stopping and generally last 1 to 2 weeks, but some people have severe symptoms that last for several months or more. The Royal College of Psychiatrists says withdrawal symptoms usually improve quickly, in days or even hours, if the antidepressant is restarted. The NHS says that if symptoms are severe, a doctor may suggest reducing the dose more slowly or going back to a higher dose before trying again. The NHS also says that once a person feels better, it is likely they will continue to take sertraline for several more months.

faqs.q: How long does sertraline take to work?
faqs.a: The NHS says people may start to feel better after 1 to 2 weeks, and that sertraline usually takes 4 to 6 weeks to work fully. The NHS says some of the common side effects gradually improve as the body gets used to the medicine. It also lists agitation, shakiness and anxiety among the early side effects of antidepressants, which generally improve with time.

faqs.q: Can sertraline be stopped once someone feels better?
faqs.a: The NHS says that once a person feels better, it is likely they will continue to take sertraline for several more months. Stopping should involve reducing the dose gradually, which helps to prevent withdrawal symptoms, and the NHS says this is normally done over several weeks or months. The UK patient leaflet says not to stop taking sertraline unless a doctor says so.

faqs.q: Can sertraline be taken in pregnancy?
faqs.a: The NHS says sertraline can be taken in pregnancy. Some studies have suggested that it might occasionally affect the development of a baby's heart, but the NHS says that if there is any risk it is small. Taken in the weeks before delivery, it can sometimes cause short-term withdrawal symptoms in the baby. The NHS says the baby will be checked after birth and given extra care if needed.

faqs.q: Can sertraline make suicidal thoughts worse?
faqs.a: MedlinePlus warns that sertraline may raise the risk of suicidal thoughts and actions in children, teenagers and young adults, and that the risk may be higher in the first few months and when the dose is increased. The NHS says that anyone who may be about to harm themselves should call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent help, NHS 111 has a mental health option (option 2), and Samaritans is free to call on 116 123 at any time.
